text.title: Junior Next Pr Checklist Template Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every junior next-PR checklist MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: Every checklist item MUST link to the review comment or diff line it came from (a permalink into the PR). An item with no origin is dropped, not kept 'because it is good advice'.

rationale.source: Google Engineering Practices, 'How to do a code review' (google.github.io/eng-practices); widely established code-review practice

rule.rationale: A checklist assembled from the mentor's general opinions is a style guide, not feedback. The permalink is what lets the junior re-read the actual mistake in context, and what stops the mentor from smuggling in items nobody ever flagged.

rule.statement: A checklist carries between 3 and 7 items. Additional candidates are parked in a `deferred` list with their permalinks and promoted only when an item is retired.

rationale.source: Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto (2009): five to nine items per pause point; working-memory limits

rule.rationale: A twenty-item list is read once and never again. Seven items fit on one screen of a PR description and can be held in mind while writing code; the deferred list keeps the mentor's observations without turning the checklist into a wall.

rule.statement: Each item MUST be phrased as a check a reviewer can answer yes or no on the next PR ("every new public function has a docstring", "the PR description links the ticket and lists the manual test"). Trait phrasing ("be more careful", "write cleaner code", "think about edge cases") is rejected.

rationale.source: Doran, 'There's a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management's goals and objectives' (1981); Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto (2009)

rule.rationale: 'Be more careful' cannot be ticked, so it is never ticked, so it is carried forever and teaches the junior that the checklist is decoration. A yes/no check either passes on the next PR or generates a concrete conversation.

rule.statement: If an item can be enforced by a linter, formatter, type checker or CI rule, the item MUST name that rule and the mentor MUST file the ticket or PR that enables it. The item stays on the checklist for at most one PR after the automation lands.

rationale.source: Google Engineering Practices, 'The Standard of Code Review' (style handled by automated tooling); widely established practice

rule.rationale: Asking a human to remember trailing whitespace or import order is a waste of the one scarce resource in mentoring: attention. Every item a machine can own frees a slot for the judgement calls only a reviewer can teach.

rule.statement: Each item MUST cite the written team standard it enforces (style-guide section, ADR, CONTRIBUTING.md anchor). If no written standard exists the item is labelled `preference:<mentor-handle>` and cannot be marked `blocking`.

rationale.source: Widely established code-review practice; Google Engineering Practices, 'The Standard of Code Review' (personal preference vs. standard)

rule.rationale: Juniors get whiplash when reviewer A's checklist contradicts reviewer B's. Citing the standard makes the item defensible to the next reviewer, and labelling preferences honestly stops one person's taste from being enforced as law.

rule.statement: Items are ordered by severity and labelled `blocking` or `should`. At most one item per checklist is `blocking`; a `blocking` item unmet on the next PR fails that review.
rule.rationale: If everything is blocking, nothing is. A single named blocker tells the junior exactly what would make the next PR fail and lets the mentor spend the rest of the review on things that are merely better.

rule.statement: Each item carries a status against the previous checklist: `new`, `carried` (with a count) or `done`. An item ticked on two consecutive PRs MUST be retired from the list. An item carried three times MUST become a pairing session, not a fourth carry.

rationale.source: Ericsson and Pool, Peak (2016), deliberate-practice feedback loops; widely established mentoring practice

rule.rationale: A checklist that only grows is a record of the junior's sins. Retiring mastered items is the visible progress that keeps them reading it, and the three-carry escalation stops the same comment appearing in every review for six months while everyone pretends the list works.

rule.statement: The junior pastes the current checklist into the next PR description and ticks each item before requesting review. The mentor verifies the ticks; the mentor never fills them. A review request with an unticked or missing checklist is sent back before code is read.

rationale.source: Google Engineering Practices, 'The CL author's guide'; self-explanation effect in learning research

rule.rationale: Self-assessment is where the learning happens: the junior who ticks 'every public function has a docstring' has just gone and checked. A mentor who ticks on their behalf turns the checklist back into a grade and the junior back into a spectator.
